sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Source control helps teams track changes to code, collaborate safely, review work, and recover earlier versions when something goes wrong.
The main mental model is: make a change → record it → review it → combine it with other work.
CompTIA wants you to recognize version management, code review, pull requests, pushes, commits, merges, and branches.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Is the scenario about tracking code history, saving a change, uploading it, reviewing it, or combining development work?
sections.callout: Save locally → commit. Send changes → push. Request review or integration → pull request. Combine branches → merge.

sections.title: Version Management
paragraphs: Version management tracks how code changes over time.
It allows teams to see previous versions, identify who changed something, compare changes, and return to an earlier state.
Think: Code has a history.
sections.callout: Developers need to track changes or restore an earlier version → version management.

sections.title: Code Review
paragraphs: A code review examines another developer's changes before they become part of the main codebase.
Reviewers may look for errors, security problems, poor logic, and inconsistent practices.
Think: Another set of eyes before the code goes live.
sections.callout: Another developer is examining proposed code changes → code review.

sections.title: Pull Request
paragraphs: A pull request asks for proposed changes from one branch to be reviewed and potentially merged into another branch.
A pull request often becomes the place where code is discussed, reviews occur, testing results appear, and approval is granted.
Think: I finished my changes. Please review them and bring them into the main code.
sections.callout: A developer requests review before merging a branch → pull request.

sections.title: Code Push
paragraphs: A code push sends locally recorded changes to a remote repository.
A developer may commit changes locally first and then push those commits to the remote system.
Think: My machine → shared repository.
sections.callout: Locally saved code changes must be uploaded to the shared repository → push.

sections.title: Code Commit
paragraphs: A commit records a set of code changes as a point in the project's history.
A commit usually represents a meaningful change. Think: Save this checkpoint in the code timeline.
sections.callout: Changes need to be recorded as a versioned checkpoint → commit.

sections.title: Code Merge
paragraphs: A merge combines changes from different branches.
For example, after a developer finishes a feature branch and receives approval, that branch may be merged into the main branch.
Think: Bring the separate work back together.
sections.callout: Changes from two branches must be combined → merge.

sections.title: Branch Management
paragraphs: A branch allows development to occur separately from another line of code.
Teams can create branches for features, fixes, and experiments while the main codebase continues operating.
Branch management includes creating, maintaining, and combining development branches.
Think: Make a side road without changing the highway yet.
sections.callout: Developers need isolated areas for separate changes → branch management.

sections.title: Source Control Flow
paragraphs: A useful exam recognition flow is: Branch → Edit → Commit → Push → Pull Request → Review → Merge.
Not every environment uses the exact same workflow, but the sequence clearly separates recording, sharing, reviewing, and combining changes.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Another developer examines changes → Code review
Request changes be reviewed or merged → Pull request
Upload local changes to a remote repository → Code push
Record a change checkpoint → Code commit
Develop separately from main code → Branch management

entries.title: Commit vs. Push
paragraphs: A commit records a change. A push sends recorded changes to a remote repository. You can commit without immediately pushing.

entries.title: Pull Request vs. Merge
paragraphs: A pull request proposes and reviews integration. A merge actually combines the code.

entries.title: Branch vs. Version
paragraphs: A branch is a separate line of development. Version management is the broader concept of tracking code changes over time.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Review another developer's work → Code review
Request review and integration → Pull request
Send local commits to remote repository → Push
